flashcards.q: Write the formula for Recall@k and Precision@k, and what question each answers.
flashcards.a: Recall@k = |relevant ∩ top-k| / |relevant| -- of everything relevant, how much did you find. Precision@k = |relevant ∩ top-k| / k -- of what you returned, how much was relevant.

flashcards.q: Write the formula for MRR and explain its key limitation.
flashcards.a: RR(query) = 1/rank_of_first_relevant_result; MRR = mean(RR). It only cares about the FIRST correct answer's position -- blind to whether more relevant documents exist further down or how many exist at all.

flashcards.q: Write the formula for MAP and explain how it differs from MRR.
flashcards.a: AP(query) = (1/|relevant docs|) * sum of Precision@k at each rank where a relevant doc appears; MAP = mean(AP). Unlike MRR, it credits finding MULTIPLE relevant documents and rewards finding them early.

flashcards.q: Write the nDCG formula and explain what the log2(i+1) discount represents.
flashcards.a: DCG@k = sum(rel_i / log2(i+1)); nDCG@k = DCG@k / IDCG@k (IDCG = DCG of the ideal ranking). log2(i+1) discounts by rank position: rank 1 contributes rel/log2(2)=rel, rank 10 contributes only rel/log2(11)~=rel/3.46 -- position matters, with diminishing sensitivity further down.

flashcards.q: Which retrieval metric should a RAG system optimize for when the generator reads the whole top-k context regardless of order?
flashcards.a: Recall@k primarily (Precision@k secondarily for noise/cost) -- getting the answer INTO the context matters more than its exact position when the LLM reads all of the top-k anyway.

flashcards.q: What size floor makes a golden set usable for gating decisions, and what happens below it?
flashcards.a: Fewer than 30 labeled queries is mostly noise -- a single query flipping swings the aggregate by several percentage points. Practical floor: 50+ queries, growing to 100-200+ as the product matures, stratified by query type and locale.

flashcards.q: State the four steps of the error-analysis loop.
flashcards.a: 1) Sample real failures. 2) Classify each by root cause (retrieval miss / ranking miss / chunking miss / generation miss). 3) Fix the DOMINANT class, not the loudest individual failure. 4) Re-measure and repeat.

A reranker only reorders candidates first-stage retrieval already surfaced; if the answer-bearing chunk never entered the candidate set, no downstream stage can recover it. You cannot rerank your way out of a recall miss -- each stage bounds what every stage after it can achieve.

flashcards.q: Why is a chunking miss easy to misdiagnose as a retrieval miss?
flashcards.a: Both produce the same downstream symptom (LLM lacks the answer or hallucinates), but a retrieval miss means the document was never found, while a chunking miss means it was found and ranked well but the chunk boundary cut the answer. Fixes are completely different (retrieval architecture vs. chunk strategy).

flashcards.q: What is ablation discipline and why does it matter when multiple pipeline changes ship together?
flashcards.a: When several changes (chunk size, embedding model, reranker) ship in one bundle, an aggregate metric improvement tells you the bundle helped, not which component did -- some could even be hurting while others mask it. Ablation isolates and measures each change independently before attributing credit.

flashcards.q: What is the typical correlation between offline retrieval metrics and online outcomes, and what does that imply?
flashcards.a: Published Pearson correlations are typically around 0.3, not 0.8+. An offline metric win is a hypothesis worth an online A/B test, not a conclusion -- ship behind experimentation where the product supports it.

flashcards.q: What golden-set annotation practice guards against a single annotator's unreliable judgment?
flashcards.a: Reconcile every case with at least two independent annotators before resolving disagreements, and give annotators worked explanations of WHY each example is relevant, not just the label, to keep future annotators consistent.

flashcards.q: Which metric fits a multi-document synthesis product (a report citing several sources), and why?
flashcards.a: MAP, or Recall@k at a higher k -- product value scales with finding multiple good sources, not just the first relevant one, which is exactly what MAP credits and MRR does not.
